title: Exceptions and recovery
goals: Keep parse failures distinct from valid zero
Return a clear outcome for every input path
vocabulary: A signal that an operation could not complete normally
Code that responds to a specified exception
A defined next step after a failure
A label stating the outcome of a processing step

blocks.text: A small parser receives duration text. Its contract permits a string representing a nonnegative integer up to 60. Invalid numeric text should return a clear status rather than crash or pretend that the duration was zero. Test both the successful and failing paths.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: try covers the operation expected to fail; except ValueError handles that known conversion failure. Returning early ends the failing path. This contract expects a string: it does not claim to handle every possible object. Spaces around an integer are accepted by int, and that behavior should be documented.

blocks.label: Predict statuses and values for "-1", " 5 " and "3.5".

blocks.text: A bare except that returns 0 hides unrelated programming errors and corrupts missing values. Catch the expected exception, preserve an error status and keep the unknown value as None. If file reading is added, handle FileNotFoundError separately with an actionable message.

Recovery must fit the task. A caller may ask for corrected input or exclude the row with a recorded reason. It must not use None as a number or claim that rejected records were successfully processed.

workbook.title: Trace success
workbook.prompt: What does parse_minutes("0") return, and why is zero allowed?
workbook.answer: A record with status ok and value 0; zero meets the inclusive range.

workbook.title: Trace two failures
workbook.answer: abc gives invalid text/None; 70 gives out of range/None. Both fail but for different reasons.

workbook.title: Repair a handler
workbook.prompt: An except block returns 0 for any failure. State two problems and a repair.
workbook.answer: It confuses failure with observed zero and may hide unrelated bugs. Catch ValueError, return an explicit status and None, then validate range.

workbook.title: Build independently
workbook.prompt: Adapt the function for count strings representing integers 0 through 10. Test "4", "0", "11", "four" and "-1" and record status/value.
workbook.answer: 4 and 0 give ok with 4 and 0; 11 and -1 give out of range/None; four gives invalid text/None. Use specific handling and explicit range checks.

workbook.title: Choose recovery
workbook.prompt: A batch has 8 valid and 2 invalid lines. What should its report include?
workbook.answer: Accepted count 8, rejected count 2 and reasons; summaries apply to accepted data. Preserve raw input for authorized correction.

teacher.background: Teach Week 27 as a two-session investigation using fictional data. A small parser receives duration text. Its contract permits a string representing a nonnegative integer up to 60. Invalid numeric text should return a clear status rather than crash or pretend that the duration was zero. Test both the successful and failing paths. Assess the three stated outcomes through the independent task, not by copying the worked result.
materials: Python 3 editor with a fresh local practice file
Paper trace table and the student workbook
Fictional input records from this lesson; no real student identifiers
sessions: Retrieve the prerequisite and explain the purpose in the opening section.
Read the worked example and diagram; ask learners to trace each step aloud.
Complete W1 and W2, then compare predictions with observed results.
Collect the guided prediction before running; discuss a mismatch and its cause.
Retrieve the main rule without showing the previous answer.
Use W3 to diagnose and repair the stated failure; rerun an earlier case.
Collect W4 independently, including code or plan, predictions and explanations, before hints.
Discuss W5 and the exit; use the fresh retry when support was needed.
